description: Christmas 2023 opens a longer run that moves through early 2024 and a December strip, using palindromes, letter positions, embedded family words, time units and self-referential counting as the field is reduced toward the one-percent questions.

s03e01.description: The Christmas special turns seasonal words, festive images and holiday conventions into the usual sequence of logic traps, forcing contestants to separate what the pictures suggest from what the wording actually asks before the final Christmas-themed one-percent puzzle.

s03e02.description: The final sequence compresses familiar units of time to their initials: seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks and months. Recognising the progression makes the missing final letter Y, for YEARS, rather than another numerical calculation.

s03e03.description: Several number and word patterns disguise simple rules before the closing sequence groups descending digits as 98, 76, 54, 32 and 10. The trick is spotting that the apparent long number is really a chain of paired countdowns.

s03e04.description: Language and visual puzzles narrow to a final two-letter answer that can complete two different words. VI fits both VICAR and VIABLE, rewarding contestants who stop trying to solve the examples separately and look for the shared beginning.

s03e05.description: Compass directions and a letter grid generate the linked words SEEN, NEW and SEWN, while a later square-based number puzzle resolves to twenty. The episode repeatedly turns tiny spelling changes into entirely different instructions.

s03e06.description: The one-percent calculation asks for the sum of every whole number from zero to one hundred. Pairing the extremes makes the shortcut visible and produces 5050, a problem that looks laborious only until the structure is noticed.

s03e07.description: HAUNT, MUMBLE, SONIC and GRANITE look unrelated until family names are found inside them: aunt, mum, son and gran. The question rewards reading across word boundaries rather than treating each word only by its dictionary meaning.

s03e08.description: A late letter-position puzzle compares ENGLAND and GERMANY and converts their shared structure into a numerical result. The intended answer is 56, reached by using where the matching letters sit rather than simply counting them.

s03e09.description: Visual and verbal logic whittle the field down before a final one-percent problem proves unusually resistant: the remaining contestants all decline to risk their winnings on it. The episode is defined less by exotic knowledge than by a final rule that refuses to reveal itself quickly.

s03e10.description: The closing number string, 248465944, only makes sense after noticing that the values are generated from the wording of the question itself. Counting letters rather than searching for a mathematical progression exposes the final four.

s03e11.description: The ladder's memorable language puzzle is the sentence MR OWL ATE MY METAL WORM. Ignoring spaces and punctuation reveals that it reads the same forwards and backwards, turning an absurd sentence into a full palindrome.

s03e12.description: One question asks which situation is impossible: marrying a cousin's cousin, a brother's widow or your widow's sister. The last option is impossible because having a widow means you are dead, a wording trap that removes a remarkable number of contestants.

s03e13.description: A body-part puzzle asks for a word that becomes the job that body part performs when one letter is added at the front. EAR becomes HEAR, a tiny change that turns anatomy into function and catches anyone searching for a more elaborate transformation.

s03e14.description: Puppet handedness, COUCH POTATO, LAD hidden inside BANGLADESH and a Tuesday bath-day clue lead into reversed body parts such as TOE, ARM, EAR and LEG. The final plays with DOUBLE and TRIPLE before the required answer is nine letter Ts.

s03e15.description: Fourteen cinema rows, digital-display segments and the word equation CAN plus TEEN equals CANTEEN precede the final image puzzle. A cube, an eight and the surrounding clues combine phonetically to produce INCUBATE.

s03e16.description: An anagram points to SWITZERLAND, repeated LORRYs must be counted and silent letters complicate HUMBUG. The final room-orientation puzzle turns handedness into a fifty-percent split, with LIZARD NEWTS among the episode's more gloriously odd word combinations.

s03e17.description: Boxing Day, the vowel pattern in 206 and a sentence involving ROB, MARK and BILL all hide instructions in ordinary language. Seasons and concealed number names follow, with the final asking contestants to count seven number words buried in the text.
